1. A clinician says “I think this patient has about a 70% chance of responding to treatment”, based on years of experience with similar cases. Which approach to probability is this, and why can it not be classical probability?

Subjective probability: a degree of belief built from judgement and experience. It cannot be classical, because classical probability needs a finite set of equally likely outcomes that can be counted, and a single patient’s response has no such symmetric structure. (Nor is it strictly empirical: no count of repeated trials was made, although the clinician’s experience is informal evidence of that kind.)

2. Write down the sample space for “number of ANC visits a woman makes, capped at 4 or more”. Which of the three axioms tells you the probabilities of its outcomes must add to 1?

S = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or more}. The outcomes do not overlap and together make up S, so by additivity (axiom 3) their probabilities add to P(S), which is 1 by axiom 2 (total probability one).

3. In a village survey, 54 of 600 adults report a diagnosis of hypertension. What is the empirical probability? Would a second survey give exactly the same number? Which law describes what happens as the survey grows?

54 ÷ 600 = 0.09. A second survey of 600 would almost certainly give a slightly different proportion, because each sample gives its own statistic for the same parameter. The (weak) law of large numbers says that as the number of people surveyed grows, the chance that the observed proportion is far from the true probability shrinks towards zero.

1. Ten independent tests, each with a 5% chance of an abnormal result. Probability that at least one is abnormal?

P(one normal) = 0.95. P(all ten normal) = 0.95¹⁰ = 0.599. P(at least one abnormal) = 1 − 0.599 = 0.401. The direct route would add P(exactly 1) through P(exactly 10), ten separate calculations; the complement needs one.

2. Two events are mutually exclusive. Explain, without using the word “exclusive”, why the addition rule simplifies.

They can never happen together, so no outcome belongs to both and P(A and B) = 0. There is no double-counted overlap to subtract, and P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

3. P(A) = 0.2, P(B) = 0.3, A and B independent. Find P(A or B).

Independence gives P(A and B) = 0.2 × 0.3 = 0.06. Then P(A or B) = 0.2 + 0.3 − 0.06 = 0.44.

1. Explain the difference between “mutually exclusive” and “independent” using a concrete pair of events.

Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen: one person’s ABO blood group being A and being B. Independent events can both happen but do not change each other’s probability: two unrelated patients in different villages each testing positive for malaria. Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are in fact dependent: knowing the blood group is A tells you with certainty it is not B.

2. How does conditional probability define independence?

A and B are independent exactly when P(A|B) = P(A): learning that B happened leaves the probability of A unchanged. Equivalently P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

3. P(underweight) = 0.25, P(recent diarrhoea) = 0.20, P(both) = 0.08. Find P(underweight | diarrhoea). Independent?

P(U|D) = P(U and D) ÷ P(D) = 0.08 ÷ 0.20 = 0.40. This is not equal to P(U) = 0.25, so the events are not independent. The product check agrees: P(U) × P(D) = 0.25 × 0.20 = 0.05 ≠ 0.08. Underweight is more common among children with recent diarrhoea than overall. (This is an association; the data do not say which causes which.)

1. Why can most positive results be false alarms when prevalence is very low?

The healthy group is far larger than the diseased group. Even a small false-positive rate, applied to that large group, produces more false positives in absolute numbers than the small diseased group produces true positives. At 1% prevalence with Se 95% and Sp 90%, 990 of 1,085 positives per 10,000 people (91%) are false.

2. Se 95%, Sp 90%, prevalence 10%. 2×2 table for 10,000 and PPV; then with odds and LR+.

Diseased 1,000: TP = 0.95 × 1,000 = 950, FN = 50. Healthy 9,000: TN = 0.90 × 9,000 = 8,100, FP = 900.

Disease No disease Total
Positive 950 900 1,850
Negative 50 8,100 8,150
Total 1,000 9,000 10,000

PPV = 950 ÷ 1,850 = 51.4% (NPV = 8,100 ÷ 8,150 = 99.4%).

Odds route: pre-test odds = 0.10 ÷ 0.90 = 0.111. LR+ = 0.95 ÷ 0.10 = 9.5. Post-test odds = 0.111 × 9.5 = 1.056. Post-test probability = 1.056 ÷ 2.056 = 0.514, the same PPV.

3. Why can an LR be carried across settings when a PPV cannot, and what limits this?

The LR is built only from Se and Sp, each computed within one true-status group, so the arithmetic contains no prevalence; you apply it to any setting’s pre-test odds. The PPV is the output of Bayes’ theorem for one particular prevalence and must be recomputed for another. The limit: Se and Sp themselves vary with disease spectrum, severity and setting (Whiting et al., 2013; Bossuyt et al., 2015), so an LR from a referral hospital may not hold in community screening.

1. Why is P(one exact value) zero for a continuous random variable, and what do you calculate instead?

Probability is spread over infinitely many values in any interval, so a single, infinitely precise value receives none of it. You calculate the probability of a range, as the area under the probability density curve between two points.

2. One discrete and one continuous random variable from clinical work.

Discrete: number of ANC visits, or number of children with a positive stool test out of 5 (countable values). Continuous: haemoglobin in g/dL, or systolic BP (any value in a range, limited only by the instrument). The test is whether the values are countable steps or points on a continuum.

3. For the ANC PMF, find P(X ≤ 1) and check E(X) = 2.9.

P(X ≤ 1) = 0.05 + 0.10 = 0.15. E(X) = 0 × 0.05 + 1 × 0.10 + 2 × 0.15 + 3 × 0.30 + 4 × 0.40 = 0 + 0.10 + 0.30 + 0.90 + 1.60 = 2.9.

1. Binomial as a sum of Bernoulli trials; mean and variance for n = 20, p = 0.8.

Code each patient 1 (recovers) or 0 (does not): each is Bernoulli(0.8). The number who recover is the sum of the 20 codes, and that sum is Binomial(20, 0.8) when the patients are independent with the same p. Expected values add: mean = 20 × 0.8 = 16. Variances of independent variables add: variance = 20 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 3.2 (SD 1.79).

2. Poisson for cancer diagnoses per month but not recoveries out of 20; why are outbreak counts overdispersed?

New cancer diagnoses in a district occur one at a time, roughly independently, at a fairly steady rate, with no fixed number of trials: the Poisson assumptions. Recoveries out of 20 have a fixed number of trials (20) and a success probability per patient, which is the binomial set-up, and the count cannot exceed 20. Measles cases are contagious: each case raises the chance of further cases, so cases arrive in bursts. Some weeks have many and others none, and the variance of weekly counts exceeds the mean (overdispersion), breaking the independence assumption.

3. λ = 2 road-traffic deaths per month. P(none) and P(at least one).

P(X = 0) = e^(−2) = 0.135. P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − 0.135 = 0.865.

1. What does z = −2 tell you, and what does it not?

The value lies 2 standard deviations below the mean of its reference distribution. If that distribution is Normal, about 2.3% of the reference population lie lower. It does not by itself mean disease or that “something is wrong”: that needs clinical context and, where relevant, an agreed cut-off (such as the WHO −2 growth cut-offs of §5.7.2.2.3).

2. Percentage beyond ±2 SD; exact multiplier for 5%.

Empirical rule: about 100 − 95 = 5%. Exactly: 100 − 95.45 = 4.55% (2.275% in each tail). Exactly 5% lies beyond ±1.96 SD.

3. Height mean 165 cm, SD 7 cm. Percentage taller than 179 cm?

z = (179 − 165) ÷ 7 = 2. P(Z > 2) = 1 − 0.9772 = 0.0228, about 2.3%.

1. Boy, 36 months, 88.0 cm; median 96.0835, SD 3.7069. HAZ, classification, centile.

HAZ = (88.0 − 96.0835) ÷ 3.7069 = −8.0835 ÷ 3.7069 = −2.18. Below −2 but not below −3: stunted (moderate), not severely stunted. Centile: P(Z < −2.18) = 0.0146, about the 1.5th centile.

2. Why can a healthy person fall outside the ALT “normal range”, and why may μ ± 1.96σ be wrong?

A reference interval is set at the 2.5th and 97.5th centiles of healthy people, so 5% of healthy people fall outside it by construction. μ ± 1.96σ gives those centiles only if the analyte is Normal in healthy people. Many analytes are skewed in healthy people (Ozarda, 2016); if ALT is, the laboratory should read the centiles directly or transform the values (for example, take logarithms), calculate the limits on that scale and transform back (Ozarda, 2016).

3. 20% anaemic; sample of 100; P(30 or more) by Normal approximation with continuity correction.

Condition: np = 20 and n(1 − p) = 80, both ≥ 5. Mean = 20; SD = √(100 × 0.2 × 0.8) = 4.0. P(X ≥ 30) ≈ P(Z > (29.5 − 20) ÷ 4) = P(Z > 2.375) = 0.009. (The exact binomial value is 0.011: the approximation is close but slightly understates this far tail.)

1. Why is t almost Normal for a large sample but not for a small one?

T = Z ÷ √(V ÷ ν), where V ÷ ν comes from the sample SD. With many degrees of freedom, s is a precise estimate of σ, V ÷ ν stays close to 1, and T behaves like Z. With few degrees of freedom, s can be well above or below σ, so the denominator varies a lot; small values of s produce large values of T, and the tails are heavier. For example, the 97.5% point is 2.776 with 4 df, 2.045 with 29 df and 1.984 with 99 df, against 1.960 for Z.

2. What are t, chi-square and F built from, and what is each used for?

All are built from independent standard Normal variables. Chi-square is a sum of ν squared standard Normals; t is a standard Normal divided by √(chi-square ÷ its df); F is the ratio of two independent chi-squares, each divided by its df. t is used for means when σ is estimated (t-tests, confidence intervals for means, regression coefficients); chi-square for tests on categorical counts and for inference on a variance; F for comparing variances and for ANOVA and overall regression tests.

3. Widening of a 95% interval for n = 10; check 2.262² = F(1, 9).

2.262 ÷ 1.960 = 1.154, so the interval is about 15% wider. 2.262² = 5.117, the 95% point of F(1, 9): the square of a t with 9 df is an F with (1, 9) df.
